Using only the latest result for each repeated eval (iteration 8 superseding iteration 5 eval 2, and iteration 7 superseding iteration 6 eval 11), 29 of 37 assertions pass in both configurations. These assertions do not discriminate skill value in these runs; they cover the shared operational behavior in git lifecycle, resume/reconciliation, conditional TDD, routine edits, read-only debugging, investigation/review, authority boundaries, inline execution, and documentation-linking.

All eight old-skill failures in the latest-per-eval evidence are assertions that require the current skill taxonomy by exact name or ownership: shaping-solutions in eval 1; governing-project-work and shaping-solutions in eval 7; managing-git in eval 8; shaping-solutions in eval 9; and all three name-migration assertions in eval 11. The evidence often records substantively aligned old-skill behavior under old names (for example apex-governance, writing-plans, or using-git-worktrees), so these results discriminate naming/migration knowledge more directly than operational behavior.

Eval 11 is explicitly name-biased by design: its three assertions require mapping brainstorming to shaping-solutions, mapping subagent-driven-development to coordinating-subagents, and identifying deleted direct lookup as a breaking migration. Its iteration 7 result (3/3 with skill versus 0/3 old skill) therefore establishes knowledge of the rename contract, not broader execution quality.

Iteration 8 corrects and supersedes iteration 5's read-only-debugging comparison. The old skill changes from 1/3 to 3/3 after the causal assertion is changed from requiring a tested hypothesis to requiring the cause remain unknown when the named failure evidence is absent, and after 'unneeded planning' is narrowed to 'unneeded durable planning.' The earlier iteration 5 advantage on eval 2 is therefore not stable evidence of a skill effect under the corrected evaluation semantics.

The read-only assertion itself is stable and non-discriminating across both eval 2 runs: it passes for both configurations in iterations 5 and 8. Under the corrected iteration 8 assertions, both configurations also request the missing causal evidence, avoid guessing, and stop before implementation.

Iteration 7 supersedes iteration 6's eval 11 candidate result: the with-skill response changes from 2/3 to 3/3 because the previously missing breaking-migration statement becomes explicit, while the old skill remains 0/3. This is evidence tied to the candidate wording change between commits, so iteration 6's 2/3 should not be treated as an additional independent run or averaged with iteration 7.

Outside exact-name assertions, the configurations repeatedly converge. Both pass every assertion in iteration 5 evals 3-6 (14/14 each), iteration 6 eval 10 (4/4 each), and iteration 8 eval 2 (3/3 each); in iteration 6 evals 7-9, the old skill passes every assertion that does not require a renamed owner (6/6).

No cross-eval difficulty or flakiness claim is supported: every benchmark records one run per configuration, all standard deviations are null, and repeated evals changed either the assertion semantics (eval 2) or the candidate commit/wording (eval 11). These are not controlled repeat runs of an unchanged condition.

Resource comparisons are unavailable across all four files: time_seconds, tokens, and tool_calls are null, timing and token metrics are marked unavailable, and the exact executor model is not exposed. The data cannot support latency, cost, tool-use, or model-variance conclusions.

The four aggregate deltas are not directly comparable as a progression: iterations 5 and 6 cover different eval sets, iterations 7 and 8 are single-eval reruns, and the candidate commits differ. In particular, iteration 7's +1.00 is entirely the name-migration eval, while iteration 8's +0.00 is entirely the corrected read-only-debugging eval.
